newsitem.title: USA: US corporate debt issuance seen on hold after data.
newsitem.headline: US corporate debt issuance seen on hold after data.

text.p: U.S. corporate treasurers contemplating debt issuance may sit out another session as they digest the latest batch of news on the economic front, and contemplate the Federal Reserve Board's next move, dealers said.

A sharp decline in the nation's unemployment rate to 5.1 percent in August, coupled with higher-than-expected average hourly earnings, raised speculation that the Fed may have to act as soon as its next September policy-setting meeting to raise interest rates, dealers said.
On Friday, the U.S. Labor Department said August unemployment fell to 5.1 percent, the lowest rate since March, 1989, when the rate was 5.0 percent.

August nonfarm payrolls were up 250,000 in August from a revised 228,000 in July. The average hourly earnings component of the report - a measure of inflation pressures - posted a better-than-expected gain of 0.5 percent versus economists' expectations of a 0.3 percent rise.

Meanwhile, dealers said investment-grade issuers who are more sensitive to sudden changes in the rate environment will probably stay off to the sidelines for now, however, high-yield, asset-backed and finance company issues, are still expected to flow into the primary market.
"Issuance is very light," said one syndicate official. "Only people who are indiffernet to levels will bring debt to market right now," said one syndicate official.

Earlier, the stronger-than-expected employment data triggered a one point selloff in the U.S. T-bond, sending Treasury yields higher. But later the long bond erased its losses to trade up a few basis points.

In addition, negative market reaction to Thursday's sharply lower initial jobless claims report had already narrowed the chances for more new issue activity as U.S. Treasury yields turned higher, dealers said.
In Thursday's business, however, Mellon Bank stirred up a little activity and priced $250 million in 11-year A2/A rated notes to yield 71 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Also, Mellon priced $100 million in two-year A1/A-plus rated bank notes to yield 6.44 percent via Chase Securities.
Dealers said recently priced debt issues have been met with very good demand by the market amid the recent drought of new corporate paper.
Despite the lack of recent debt issuance, a number of banks are rumored to have positioned themselves to issue debt in the event an opportunistic rate environment emerges, syndicate sources said.
"There's talk of a lot of bank paper coming to market," said one syndicate source. "A calendar seems to be building, but a lot depends on the rate environment."
Among names circulating in the market are Wells Fargo, Signet Bank, Nationsbank, Key Bank, Australia/New Zealand Bank and Argentaria Bank with a $250 million yankee offering, sources said.
In the government market, the benchmark U.S. Treasury bond is up 21/32 at 95-22/32 to yield 7.10 percent, compared with Thursday's close at 7.15 percent.
